title: We Few, We Happy Few
text:
In Shakespeare's play, King Henry V of England had invaded France, and by the morning of the battle of Agincourt in 1415 his army was sick, hungry and badly outnumbered by the French. In the English camp, the Earl of Westmoreland wished aloud that they had even ten thousand more of the men sitting idle back in England.

The king overheard and disagreed. If they were going to die, he said, they were enough for their country to lose. If they were going to live, the fewer men, the greater each one's share of honor. He did not wish for one man more. In fact, he ordered that any soldier who had no stomach for the fight should be allowed to leave, with a passport and money for his journey. He did not want to die in the company of anyone who feared to die alongside him.

That day, he reminded them, was the feast of Saint Crispin. Those who fought and came home safe would stand tall whenever the day was named, show their scars to their neighbors, and be remembered as long as the story was told. "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers," he said, for whoever shed his blood with him that day would be his brother, however humble his birth.

The English army went into battle, and in the play it won.
lesson: Shared hardship can turn a group into a band of brothers when the leader stands with them as an equal. Give people a reason to be proud of being few rather than wishing for more.
people: King Henry V, the Earl of Westmoreland, the English army
location: London, England (play set at Agincourt, France)
source: William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act 4, Scene 3
caveat: The speech is Shakespeare's invention, not a record of what Henry said at the real battle.
